1.title: GenAI Capabilities, Limits and Business Value
1.text: Welcome to Module five: Gen A I Capabilities, Limits and Business Value. This module covers task statement two point two. You will learn what generative A I does well, where it falls short, how to choose a model, and how to show that a solution pays for itself. The exam gives you a situation and asks you to name the strength, the limit, the factor or the metric.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. Name the advantages of generative A I. Identify its disadvantages: hallucinations, interpretability, inaccuracy and nondeterminism. List the factors for choosing a model. And pick business value metrics, such as R O I, efficiency and conversion rate.

1.title: Case Check-In: Cedar and Salt Weighs Its Pilots
1.text: At Cedar and Salt Travel, the leaders are excited about the review-summary tool and the booking assistant. The risk team asks what can go wrong, and how they will know it works. Engineers must choose a model, and finance wants proof of value. Your job is to separate real strengths from real limits, and to name the right measures.

1.title: What Generative AI Does Well
1.text: Start with the strengths. Adaptability: one model handles many tasks, steered by prompts. Responsiveness: it answers in seconds, at any time of day. Conversational ability: it understands natural language and replies in kind. And content generation: it drafts text, images, code and summaries. Together these speed up work, and make A I easier to use for people who are not experts. Exam tip: adaptable, responsive, conversational and able to generate content are the advantages to remember.

1.title: Hallucinations
1.text: The best-known limit is the hallucination. A hallucination is an incorrect or misleading output from a foundation model. Causes include poor or limited training data, overfitting, a limited context window, and ambiguous language. The effects can be bad decisions, misinformation and security risks. You can reduce hallucinations with Retrieval Augmented Generation, or R A G, with specific prompts, with Guardrails and with monitoring. But they cannot be fully removed. Exam tip: a confident, wrong answer is a hallucination, and grounding with R A G helps most.

1.title: Other Limits: Nondeterminism, Interpretability and Inaccuracy
1.text: There are other limits to know. Nondeterminism means the same prompt can give different answers, because the model samples the next token. A lower temperature gives steadier output. Interpretability means it is hard to explain why the model gave an answer; citations, evaluations and human review help. Inaccuracy means answers can be wrong, outdated or biased; grounding, testing and monitoring help. Generative A I also needs care with private data and cost control. Exam tip: different answers to the same prompt mean nondeterminism, and hard to explain means interpretability.

1.title: Factors for Choosing a Model
1.text: When you choose a model, consider seven factors. Model type and modality: text, image, audio or multi-modal. Performance requirements: quality on your task. Capabilities: reasoning, languages, tool use and context length. Constraints and compliance: data residency, license and the rules you must meet. Cost: the price per token, plus the cost to run. Latency: how fast answers must arrive. And model complexity, because bigger is not always better. Exam tip: test candidate models on your own task, and do not choose by size alone.

1.title: Quality, Cost and Speed Trade-Offs
1.text: Models trade quality against cost and speed. A larger model is often more capable, but it usually costs more and answers more slowly. A smaller model is cheaper and faster, and it may be good enough for a narrow task. Match the model to the task: summarizing reviews needs less than complex planning. Evaluate a few models on real examples from your business, and revisit the choice as new models appear. Exam tip: the best model is the cheapest and fastest one that meets the quality bar.

1.title: Business Value and Metrics
1.text: Now business value. Return on investment compares the value gained with the cost. Efficiency is the time or effort saved per task. Conversion rate is the share of visitors who complete a goal, such as a booking. Average revenue per user is revenue divided by users. Customer lifetime value is the total expected revenue from a customer over time. Accuracy is how often answers are right. And cross-domain performance is quality across different tasks and topics. Exam tip: match the metric to the goal: sales means conversion, payback means R O I, and speed means efficiency.

1.title: Measuring Value Honestly
1.text: Measuring value takes care, and this slide goes beyond the guide. Track cost and value together: cost per outcome is the A I cost divided by a business value metric. Many things move revenue, so attributing it to A I is hard; use tests against a control group. Be careful with output counts, such as lines of code, because they can be gamed. Include quality and customer feedback, not only speed. And review the numbers regularly, not once. Exam tip: one number is never enough, so pair a value metric with a cost metric.

1.title: What the Exam Asks: Capabilities, Limits and Value
1.text: Here is how the exam frames this module. An advantage: adaptability, responsiveness, conversational ability or content generation. A limit: hallucination, nondeterminism, interpretability or inaccuracy. A fix: R A G and Guardrails for hallucinations, and a lower temperature for steadiness. A model factor: type, performance, capability, compliance, cost, latency or complexity. And a business metric: R O I, efficiency, conversion rate, average revenue per user or customer lifetime value. Exam tip: name the situation first, then the limit, factor or metric.

1.title: Design Check: Cedar and Salt's Pilot Review
1.text: Now a design check. Cover the right column and name the answer. The assistant invents a cancellation policy: a hallucination, so ground it with R A G and Guardrails. The same question gets two different replies: nondeterminism, so lower the temperature. Nobody can say why it answered that way: an interpretability limit, so add citations and review. Chat must be fast and cheap: a smaller model, tested on real chats. Leaders want proof it sells more trips: conversion rate. And finance wants payback: R O I and cost per outcome. Pause the video if you want more time.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. The advantages are adaptability, responsiveness, conversational ability and content generation. The limits are hallucinations, nondeterminism, interpretability and inaccuracy. The fixes are R A G, Guardrails, prompts, monitoring and human review. The model factors are type, performance, capabilities, compliance, cost, latency and complexity. And value is measured with R O I, efficiency, conversion rate, average revenue per user and customer lifetime value, together with cost per outcome.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Which of the following is an advantage of generative A I for a business? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: it can converse in natural language and generate new content on request. Generative A I is adaptable, responsive and conversational. It does not guarantee correctness, it still benefits from human review, and it has costs.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Cedar and Salt's assistant confidently quotes a cancellation policy that does not exist. What is this called, and what helps most? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: a hallucination, which is reduced by grounding answers with R A G. An incorrect or invented output from a foundation model is a hallucination. Retrieval Augmented Generation grounds answers in real company documents, and Guardrails and monitoring help too.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Select two. Which two are limitations of generative A I solutions? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and C. Hallucinations and nondeterminism are well-known limits, along with limited interpretability and inaccuracy. The other options are false statements about generative A I.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. The booking chat must answer within about a second and the budget is tight. Which approach to choosing a model fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: test smaller, faster models on real chats, and pick one that meets the quality bar. Latency and cost are selection factors, and a smaller model may be good enough for a narrow task. Evaluating candidates on real examples shows which one meets the quality bar at the lowest cost.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Leaders want evidence that the new assistant leads more visitors to complete a booking. Which metric measures this directly? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A, conversion rate, the share of visitors who complete a booking. It shows sales impact. Model size, context window and temperature describe the model, not business results.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all five answers. Question one: C. Question two: B. Question three: A and C. Question four: D. Question five: A. That completes Module five. Next, Module six looks at the A W S services and infrastructure for building generative A I applications, and what they cost.
